Evidence shows Salesforce publishes its own MCP server (salesforcecli/mcp) so external tools can call Salesforce, but there is no evidence that Salesforce Sales Cloud/Agentforce can act as an MCP client—i.e., ingest and use tools from third-party MCP servers within its agents or workflows.

Salesforce maintains an official MCP server repo (salesforcecli/mcp) alongside its official CLI, directly enabling agent connectivity via MCP, though evidence is limited to a repo pointer without deeper usage detail.

Salesforce markets Agentforce agents that can be invoked/built for natural-language task automation, has an official MCP server and CLI supporting agent creation (sf agent create), but evidence is largely vendor marketing plus dev tooling rather than proof that end users can operate the core CRM via natural-language commands directly; no independent confirmation of conversational operation quality.

Salesforce provides an official, actively maintained CLI (@salesforce/cli, installable via npm) with rich commands spanning org management, data queries, Apex testing, and even agent creation (sf agent create), plus a plugin developer guide for extensibility—confirmed by both GitHub evidence and an independent probe.

The evidence shows Salesforce's general platform/security features and CLI/agent tooling exist, but there is no mention of scoped or least-privilege API credential issuance specifically for agents (e.g., connected apps with permission scoping, named credentials, or agent-specific OAuth scopes).

Salesforce offers official SDK-like tooling: the salesforcecli/cli (npm install, org create, apex test, agent create), an official MCP server, and API discovery docs, plus community confirmation of solid developer tooling (VS Code extensions, CLI, deployment paths). Salesforce's CLI (sf data query, sf apex run test, sf agent create) and API access suggest programmatic/bulk data handling is possible, and Agentforce agents are pitched for automating repetitive tasks at scale, but the evidence pack lacks any direct mention of bulk API, mass update tools, or explicit bulk-record processing capabilities.

Salesforce supports automation via Flow/Process Builder-style workflows and AI agents deployed 'across every stage of the deal cycle,' but the evidence pack mostly shows marketing claims about AI-powered insights and agent deployment rather than concrete rule-trigger configuration details or hands-on validation of event-driven automation.

The evidence pack shows Salesforce CLI, Agentforce, and automation/AI features generally, but nothing specifically addresses scheduling recurring jobs or workflows for an AI-native user (e.g., cron-like triggers, scheduled flows, or agent scheduling APIs). Salesforce docs mention AI automatically syncing 'Emails, Events, and Contacts' (salesforce-docs-8), which implies calendar/meeting sync into CRM records, but there is no specific evidence describing meetings appearing on contact/deal timelines or detailing calendar integration setup, and no community validation of this feature.

No evidence explicitly describes creating custom objects/fields/relationships, but developer tooling (sf CLI, scratch orgs, Apex tests, data queries) and strong community testimony about Salesforce's deep customizability ('king of customizations', LWC local dev, VS Code extensions) imply this capability exists, though not directly documented in the pack.

The evidence pack mentions generic Lead/Account/Contact/Opportunity management but contains no specific mention of duplicate detection, matching rules, or merge functionality for contacts or accounts.

The Salesforce CLI supports data queries (sf data query) and APIs exist for pulling records, offering a technical path to export data, but there is no evidence of a bulk/open-format full data export or a documented 'leave with your data' workflow; no explicit data-portability or export-all documentation is present.

Twenty offers the building blocks needed: an MCP server and GraphQL/REST API exposing deals, companies, and people (twenty-docs-32, twenty-docs-8, twenty-docs-22), automatic email/calendar sync to CRM records (twenty-docs-4, twenty-docs-52, twenty-docs-58), and permission-scoped AI agents that can query and enrich records autonomously (twenty-docs-5, twenty-docs-18, twenty-docs-56, twenty-docs-19). However, there's no documented pre-built 'account brief' template or workflow combining these into a single meeting-prep output — it would require custom agent/workflow assembly — and community feedback flags rough edges ('pretty alpha-version... ran into quite a few small issues') that tempers confidence in production reliability.

Twenty ships the necessary building blocks — an MCP server (twenty-docs-32), AI agents that can 'execute multi-step tasks autonomously' including enriching records (twenty-docs-5, twenty-docs-56), workflows that can chain an 'AI Agent' step with record operations (twenty-docs-13), and automatic email/calendar syncing onto CRM records (twenty-docs-4, twenty-docs-52, twenty-docs-58) plus REST/GraphQL APIs for programmatic updates (twenty-docs-8, twenty-docs-25). However, no evidence explicitly shows an agent parsing email/meeting content to update deal stage and next-steps end-to-end, and one community report flags the product as 'pretty alpha-version' with rough edges in the API (twenty-comm-1), so this is a plausible but unproven composite capability.

Twenty's pricing page lists 'MCP server | Yes | Yes | Yes' across all tiers, indicating some MCP support exists, but no docs detail whether this lets users plug in external MCP servers for tool use or simply exposes Twenty itself as an MCP server, and no hands-on/community confirmation exists.

The pricing page explicitly lists 'MCP server | Yes | Yes | Yes' confirming an official MCP server is offered across plans, and Twenty's AI agent framework docs describe permission-scoped agents operating within the CRM, which aligns with MCP-style agent connectivity. Twenty offers an AI chatbot for natural-language querying of CRM data and AI agents that can autonomously execute multi-step tasks (enrichment, answering questions) within permissions, plus an MCP server listed in pricing tiers. Twenty offers a developer-first REST/GraphQL API with auto-generated docs, a Metadata API for programmatic schema changes, and a CLI (create-twenty-app) for scaffolding apps in React/TypeScript, plus an MCP server listed in pricing tiers — but the evidence never mentions an official client SDK (e.g., JS/Python library) that AI-native builders could import directly.
